item.title: Trump establishes US space academy as Artemis II crew receives Space Medal of Honor - ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
item.description:
Trump establishes US space academy as Artemis II crew receives Space Medal of Honor

Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen were honored.

President Donald Trump on Friday bestowed the Congressional Space Medal of Honor on the Artemis II crew, marking their historic achievement during a ceremony at Johnson Space Center in Houston.

The crew -- NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover and Christina Koch and Canadian Space Agency astronaut Jeremy Hansen -- traveled farther into deep space than anyone else in history during their trip around the Moon in April. What they learned during their test flight will help NASA return astronauts to the lunar surface as early as 2028.

"We gather here on these storied grounds to celebrate the immense courage and service of four intrepid space heroes whose sense of daring and adventure led them further from Earth than anyone has ever traveled before," Trump said.

Joined at the event by NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman, the president told a story about being in an important meeting with "the biggest people in the country, maybe some of the biggest people in the world" when someone asked to watch the Artemis II mission.

"You would, really? Right in the middle of our meeting. You want to watch?" Trump recalled saying at the time. He said they had a television set pulled up for the group to watch, adding that "everybody was spellbound."

The president used Friday's occasion to sign an executive order establishing the U.S. Space Academy, a national academy similar to the service academies for the armed forces, such as West Point and the Air Force Academy.

"It will serve both the United States Space Force as well as NASA and the civilian spaceflight industry, and it'll attract, train and graduate the very best of our nation," Trump said.

A location for the new academy will be chosen shortly, according to the president.

During the ceremony, the president personally placed the medal around the necks of each astronaut as they were recognized for their work during the mission.

After receiving his medal, an emotional Wiseman, the commander of the Artemis II mission, spoke about the scale of the joint effort the mission required.

"We wear these four medals, and we are going to wear them with pride. But please know, it is not pride for ourselves that we feel, and I truly mean that," he said. "It is pride for the grit that our families had when we left this planet. It is pride for that team, this NASA team, that sent us on this mission. And it is pride for the international community that stood alongside us, got this vehicle ready, operated and cheered us on."

Glover, the Artemis II pilot, then presented Trump with an official NASA blue flight jacket, saying the crew wanted to make good on its promise to him when they were in the Oval Office.

"To the Artemis crew II, you stand here incredibly deserving of this recognition. Thank you for showing us the moon again, for showing the world your humanity and for passing your knowledge and the baton to the astronauts who will follow in your very accomplished footsteps. There are no finer humans we could have sent as our ambassadors to the stars," NASA's Isaacman said during the event.

With NASA's astronaut corps seated on stage, Apollo 17 astronaut and former Sen. Harrison Schmitt, a Republican from New Mexico, kicked off the event by speaking about his 1972 mission -- the last mission of the Apollo program.

"Apollo 17's success, as the success of all the other missions was owed to the patriotic dedication, the courage, the competence of young men and women, young men and women, who designed and built and managed and trained and planned each of the Mercury, Gemini and Apollo missions. It was an extraordinary privilege for me to be part of that."

NASA Deputy Administrator Matt Anderson said Apollo pioneers like Schmitt "handed the baton" to the men and women working on the space shuttle program, which built the International Space Station.

"Early this year, the Artemis II crew added their names to that history. They carried humanity around the world, around the moon, for the first time in more than 50 years. Demonstrated that America is ready to return and paved the way for those who will follow," Anderson said.

He also spoke about what's at stake for NASA and the U.S. space program in the years to come.

"The second space race has begun, and right now, America is on the shot clock. Our national security, the prestige of our nation and the dreams of millions of Americans are riding on our ability to get the job done."

Congress authorized the granting of the Congressional Space Medal of Honor in 1969, proclaiming that "The President may award, and present in the name of Congress, a medal of appropriate design, which shall be known as the Congressional Space Medal of Honor, to any astronaut who in the performance of his duties has distinguished himself by exceptionally meritorious efforts and contributions to the welfare of the Nation and of mankind."

Since then, only 34 astronauts have received the honor, including the Artemis II crew. The first recipients of the award in 1978 included Neil Armstrong, Frank Borman, Pete Conrad, John Glenn, Virgil "Gus" Grissom and Alan Shepard.
item.source: ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos

item.title: Artemis II astronauts receive nation's highest space honor for their successful moonshot - The Guardian
item.description:
The Artemis II astronauts who flew around the moon in April received the US’s highest space honor on Friday.

Donald Trump presented the Congressional Space Medal of Honor to the three Americans and one Canadian whose lunar flyby for the US space agency Nasa set a new distance record for humanity.

Nasa’s administrator, Jared Isaacman, and other dignitaries took part in the packed ceremony at Houston’s Johnson Space Center, home to mission control. The president used the occasion to announce the creation of a US space academy for the nation’s space force as well as Nasa and the commercial space community.

“Space is the hot thing,” Trump told the crowd, adding that the academy’s location has yet to be determined.

Cmdr Reid Wiseman, pilot Victor Glover, and mission specialists Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen, a Canadian, became the first astronauts to travel to the moon in more than half a century, coming within 4,067 miles (6,545km) while test-driving Nasa’s new Orion capsule. They were the first to launch onboard Nasa’s new moon rocket, a 30-story behemoth that had soared only once before from Florida’s Kennedy Space Center.

While they didn’t stop at the moon, the four set the stage for next year’s Artemis III docking rehearsal in orbit around Earth. Artemis IV’s moon landing by two astronauts, near the lunar south pole, could follow as soon as 2028.

Trump said Americans will land back on the moon before his second presidency ends. Mars is next – “very shortly”, he said.

The president called the newest recipients “four intrepid space heroes”. He pointed out that they did not do it alone, thanking all who contributed to the Artemis II mission.

“There are no finer humans we could have sent as our ambassadors to the stars,” Isaacman added.

Wiseman and his crew are in good company, with only 30 astronauts receiving the prestigious honor before them. Many of the recipients were honored posthumously following their spaceflight-related deaths.

Apollo 11 commander Neil Armstrong – whose phrase “that’s one step for man, one giant leap for mankind” gripped the world when he became the first person to walk on the moon on 20 July 1969 – was the first to receive the Congressional Space Medal of Honor.

President Jimmy Carter awarded six of these medals in 1978, which also went to Alan Shepard, the first American in space; John Glenn, the first American in orbit; and Apollo 8 commander Frank Borman, whose 1968 mission marked humanity’s first lunar voyage.

The most recent recipients were Doug Hurley and Bob Behnken, the first astronauts to launch aboard a SpaceX rocket. Coming nine years after the space shuttle program’s close, their 2020 test flight to the International Space Station restored the US’s ability to launch crews from home soil. Joe Biden awarded them the medals in 2023, during the third year of his presidency.

Dozens of astronauts participated in the ceremony, including Apollo 17 moonwalker Harrison Schmitt, who is now 91 – and the four men assigned to Nasa’s upcoming Artemis III mission.

Schmitt noted that his mission – Apollo’s last moonshot – was the most productive lunar exploration yet.

“Soon to be surpassed by Artemis,” he said of active astronauts standing behind him.

Nasa plans a sustainable moon base staffed by astronauts and robots near the lunar south pole, where permanently shadowed craters are thought to hold tons of frozen water that could be turned into rocket fuel and drinking water. China is eyeing the same region.

“The second space race has begun,” Nasa’s deputy administrator, Matthew Anderson, said.

As the two-hour ceremony came to a close, the Artemis II astronauts presented Trump with his own blue flight jacket complete with space patches, which they had promised him while visiting him in the Oval Office after their mission.

The president then hustled over to mission control to call the three US astronauts onboard the International Space Station. He informed them of the new US space academy, then briefly handed the phone to two of their spouses for a quick hello.

item.title: NASA’s Artemis II Crew Receives Congressional Space Medal of Honor - NASA (.gov)
item.description:
From left to right: NASA astronauts Victor Glover and Christina Koch, CSA (Canadian Space Agency) astronaut Jeremy Hansen, and NASA astronaut Reid Wiseman receive the Congressional Space Medal of Honor from President Donald J. Trump on Aug. 28, 2026, for their service during the Artemis II mission.

The Congressional Space Medal of Honor was authorized by Congress in 1969 to recognize an astronaut who in the performance of duties has distinguished himself or herself by exceptionally brave and meritorious efforts, and contributions to the welfare of the nation and humanity. There now are 34 recipients of the award since the beginning of the space program, including the crews of Apollo 1, Challenger, and Columbia who received the award posthumously.

Image credit: NASA/John Kraus

item.title: Trump awards medals to Artemis II crew for moon flyby - NBC News
item.description:
Trump awards medals to Artemis II crew for moon flyby

The majority of Americans disapprove of the Iran war and President Donald Trump’s handling of the conflict, polling shows.

What to know today

  • TRUMP HONORS ASTRONAUTS:President Donald Trump today awarded the Congressional Space Medal of Honor to the crewmembers of the Artemis II, who made history this year on their mission around the moon. During his remarks, the president announced the creation of the U.S. Space Academy.
  • HEGSETH MULLS 2028:Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has told close friends and associates that he is considering a run for president in 2028, according to two people familiar with the conversations.
  • IRAN WAR POLLING:Americans remain sour on the Iran war and Trump’s handling of the conflict after six months, and they continue to say they oppose the military action, according to an NBC News review of public polling.
  • MARCH ON WASHINGTON:House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., and other Democratic lawmakers spoke alongside civil rights, faith and labor leaders at the March on Washington today.

White House teleprompter operator ordered to pay $172K for placing prediction market bets on Trump’s speeches

A teleprompter operator for President Donald Trump who made online prediction trades based on information from upcoming speeches has been ordered to pay $172,000, a federal agency said tonight.

Gabriel Perez used “material, nonpublic information” he obtained through his job to place “trades” on a prediction market, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission said in a news release.

Perez was ordered to pay the money he made in profits, $107,539.02, as well as a civil penalty of $65,000.

John Moore / Getty Images file

Trump says he’ll visit Pentagon, rather than Ground Zero, for 9/11 ceremony

President Donald Trump will appear at the Pentagon to mark the 25th anniversary of the attacks on Sept. 11, 2001, instead of visiting Ground Zero in New York City.

Asked about why he would not be commemorating the anniversary in his hometown, Trump told reporters today, “Because I’m going to the Pentagon.”

Vice President JD Vance is instead expected to attend the event in New York City, according to a senior administration official. Other officials will attend a ceremony in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, on the day, the official added.

The New York Times first reported that Trump would travel to the Pentagon on 9/11, writing Thursday that the president had initially wanted to go to New York City but decided against it when organizers would not allow him to speak during the Ground Zero program, which traditionally does not permit speeches.

= Yuki Iwamura / AP

Leader of the Seneca Nation demands Trump reinstate Lake Ontario's name

The leader of the Seneca Nation today condemned Trump's executive order to rename Lake Ontario to "Lake America," urging the president to reinstate its longstanding name with Indigenous roots.

Seneca Nation President J. Conrad Seneca said in a statement today that Trump's order showed "blatant disrespect" to all Indigenous people, calling it "starkly un-presidential and demeaning to his office and his standing as the leader of the free world.”

"Long before the United States existed, and before settlers brought the English language to our lands, our Seneca and Haudenosaunee ancestors traveled Lake Ontario and surrounding waterways for many reasons, including diplomacy among our nations. Now, we are seeing the exact opposite of diplomacy," Seneca wrote in a statement.

Seneca said that in the nation's traditional Seneca language, the lake's name is sga:nyodai:yoh, meaning ‘beautiful lake.’

Seneca said the renaming goes against the 1794 Treaty of Canandaigua, an agreement signed by the Haudenosaunee and Seneca nations and President George Washington "promising to live in peace and friendship with one another."

"President Trump’s aggression toward our culture with his Executive Order violates that peace, friendship and commitments of the Canandaigua treaty," Seneca wrote. “The President cannot assert ownership over our culture or erase it through irresponsible political action."

He wrote that Seneca Nation is calling local, state and federal representatives to stand against Trump's order "regardless of political party."

U.S. has entered deal with Venezuela to take control of 65 billion barrels of oil reserves, Trump says

President Donald Trump announced today that the U.S. had entered into an agreement with Venezuela to take control of the country’s 65 billion barrels of oil reserves.

“BREAKING NEWS: The United States of America has just entered into an Agreement with the Country of Venezuela on, THE BIGGEST OIL DEAL IN WORLD HISTORY! At my direction, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, working closely with Highly Respected Interim President of Venezuela, Delcy Rodriguez, and, through a partnership with private business, have secured majority U.S. control of more than 65 BILLION BARRELS of proven Oil Reserves in Venezuela, at no cost to the American Taxpayer,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

Trump added that the transaction “MORE THAN DOUBLES American Oil Reserves.”

A sculpture in front of the Caracas headquarters of Petroleos de Venezuela, the state-owned oil and natural gas company, in 2022. Miguel Zambrano / AFP via Getty Images file

Kentucky woman indicted on charges she damaged the World War II Memorial in Washington

A Kentucky woman has been indicted by a federal grand jury on charges that she intentionally damaged The World War II Memorial on the National Mall in Washington, D.C.

Melissa Farris is scheduled to be arraigned next week on two felony counts. Grand jurors indicted her today on charges of destroying the veterans’ memorial and destroying government property.

An attorney for Farris didn’t immediately respond to an email seeking comment on Friday.

Farris, of Elizabethtown, Kentucky, is suspected of spray painting the words “Clean hands dirty $” on the monument and filling a fountain with bubbles on Aug. 13. She was ordered released after her initial court appearance on Aug. 17.

Milo Yiannopoulos arrested by ICE

Milo Yiannopoulos, a self-described libertarian and professional internet troll who became known for his controversial right-wing political views, is in ICE custody.

A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security told NBC News that ICE arrested Yiannopoulos, a United Kingdom national, today at the Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport in Kenner, Louisiana.

The DHS spokesperson said Yiannopoulos legally entered the U.S. on May 14, 2019, through New York City, but then “chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws.”

Yiannopoulos was taken into ICE custody Thursday after “failing to show up for his immigration hearing” on July 22, prompting an immigration judge to issue a final order of removal against him, according to the spokesperson. “He will remain in ICE custody pending removal,” the spokesperson added.

Pete Hegseth is talking about a possible run for president in 2028, sources say

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has told close friends and associates that he is considering a run for president in 2028, according to two people familiar with the conversations.

Daniel Heuer / Bloomberg via Getty Images

ICE plans to buy robot ‘dogs’ for some immigration enforcement operations

Immigration Customs and Enforcement plans to spend as much as $2 million to purchase robot “dogs” that the agency would use in immigration enforcement operations, according to a government funding document reviewed by NBC News.

A senior Department of Homeland Security official confirmed ICE is planning to purchase the robots. They would be used in situations where it may be unsafe for an officer to go into a building or area, the official said.

Kevin Dietsch / Getty Images

GOP Sen. Susan Collins asks Trump administration to restart trade talks with Canada

Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, who faces a difficult re-election battle this fall, is asking Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer to restart trade negotiations with Canada.

J. Scott Applewhite / AP

“For Mainers, commerce with Canada is a regular occurrence," Collins wrote in a letter today to the Trump administration officials. "Maine borders only one state, but shares a 611-mile border with Canada. The consequences of Canada’s retaliatory tariffs are severe for Maine businesses, including our heritage industries.”

Collins has objected to the tariffs, warning that they’ll harm Maine, a border state that trades heavily with Canada. In her letter, the senator estimated $170 million worth of Maine goods will be subject to Canada's tariffs, with 62% coming from forestry products. She also praised Canada's decision to drop its initially planned tariff on seafood and fish products, which she said would have resulted in $200 million in duties on Maine's lobster industry.

“Maine’s economy is uniquely intertwined with Canada, and the consequences of an escalating trade dispute will be felt by American families, businesses, workers, and communities across the state," Collins wrote. "Thousands of American jobs and businesses across a variety of sectors are at risk."

Trump administration appealing ruling involving mail-in ballots

The Trump administration has appealed a federal judge's order yesterday blocking a Postal Service regulation that would have required the USPS to deliver mail-in ballots only to people on an eligible voters list.

Logan Cyrus / AFP via Getty Images file

U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani found the regulation is most likely unlawful because the president cannot insert the federal government into elections without the express authorization of Congress.

The recently finalized measure would implement a key provision of the president’s executive order directing the Postal Service to, among other things, track mail-in ballots and potentially reject those submitted by people not on a federal list of eligible voters.

“The court finds plaintiffs likely to succeed on the merits of their claims,” she said.

How much has the Iran war cost so far? Tracking the human and financial toll

Shortly after the U.S. and Israel launched strikes on Iran in late February, Trump said he expected the war would wrap up in four to five weeks. The conflict has lasted much longer and taken a far greater toll than officials projected.

A dignified transfer at Dover Air Force Base last month. Daniel Heuer / Bloomberg via Getty Images

Elon Musk’s super PAC begins pouring money into the midterms online

Billionaire Elon Musk’s super PAC launched digital ads in key Senate battlegrounds this month, the group’s first significant advertising spending since last year’s state Supreme Court race in Wisconsin.

The new digital ads are running in Maine, Michigan and New Hampshire target specific lists of people and urge viewers to register to vote, according to a review of Meta political ad data. Some ads are generic, featuring reminders that the Senate races in their states could decide control of the chamber.

Alex Brandon / AP file

Sen. Bernie Sanders says 'Dr. King's dream is under threat'

Speaking at an event in Washington marking the 63rd anniversary of the March on Washington, Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., said Trump was threatening democracy and the right to vote.

Alex Wong / Getty Images

"Donald Trump is an authoritarian who is deliberately trying to destroy faith in American democracy, create confusion, sow mistrust in our elections and make it harder for Americans to vote. But Dr. King's dream is under threat in other ways as well," Sanders told attendees. "Dr. King understood that political freedom and economic freedom are inseparable, and that is why the March on Washington was not simply a march for voting rights, as enormously important as that was. It was the March on Washington for jobs and freedom."

He added, "it's not only voting rights that are under assault today. That part of Dr. King's dream-the dream of genuine economic freedom-is all. also under unprecedented attack. Today, we have more income and wealth inequality than at any moment in American history."

Judge denies latest Trump bid to move hush money case to federal court

A federal judge in New York has again blocked the president from trying to move the hush money case that saw him convicted of 34 counts of falsifying business records to federal court.

“President Trump must show that 'he acted diligently and without undue delay to remove the case based on' new grounds, here, principally the issuance of the United States Supreme Court’s decision in Trump v. United States, in order to 'show good cause for the untimely filing at issue,'” U.S. District Judge Alvin Hellerstein wrote, adding that the president had failed to do so.

Stormy Daniels; Michael Cohen AP file

The judge found Trump had waited too long after the high court's ruling on presidential immunity to try to move the case, and that he only attempted to do so after it became clear the state court was going to reject his immunity arguments.

Trump had pleaded not guilty to the criminal charges and is appealing his conviction.

Hellerstein, who'd rejected Trump's earlier attempts to move the case, also ripped the argument that the trial testimony of his former White House aides Hope Hicks and Madeleine Westerhout and former personal lawyer Michael Cohen infringed on presidential immunity.

“They do not,” Hellerstein wrote. “Paying hush money to an adult film star or engaging in a cover-up of an embarrassment are not subsumed in presidential immunity.”

“There is no way that discussions regarding hush money payments to cover up the President’s relations with Stormy Daniels could be an official act," Hellerstein ruled, referring to the adult film actor, who alleged an affair with Trump years earlier. "An affair, or a cover-up of an affair, is not within the ’outer perimeter’ of the President’s official responsibilities,” .

Trump has repeatedly denied the affair allegation.

The president's attorneys also argued in court that four of Trump’s online posts should be considered an official act.

But the judge wrote that the tweets “discussed Cohen’s role as the President’s personal attorney and stated that the matter with Stormy Daniels was 'a private contract' between Cohen and Daniels,” meaning that each was "an unofficial communication."

“Trump used his personal Twitter account, where he regularly communicated both official and unofficial statements," he wrote.

Hellerstein added the prosecution arose from private conduct, surrounding the reimbursement of hush money payments to the adult film star.

“That conduct, and the challenged evidence, bears no substantive relation to his position in federal office," he wrote. "To consider these facts to be ’relating to’ a federal office would give the words a definition that is 'so broad that it is meaningless.'"

Attorneys for the president filed a notice that he was appealing Hellerstein's order shortly after it was handed down.

Judge in birthright citizenship case skeptical of government's claims

A federal judge in Maryland is allowing Trump’s renewed effort to limit birthright citizenship to move forward, but likely only for the next few days.

At a hearing this morning, U.S. District Judge Deborah Boardman pushed back against a Justice Department lawyer's assertion that no imminent action was being taken as a result of Trump's latest order targeting birthright citizenship.

The new order is focused on restricting automatic citizenship to children born to adults working for foreign embassies, as well as anyone who would fall under the definition of an ”alien enemy” of the United States.

She denied immigration group CASA’s request to block the order, but only because of what is really a technicality: The original complaint in the case focused on Trump’s 2025 birthright citizenship executive order, not the August 2026 order.

The judge called the latest EO “unprecedented” and said it contradicts the ruling handed down by the Supreme Court earlier this year on a prior executive order on the issue. It appears the president is “trying to rewrite the carveouts to birthright citizenship with the stroke of a pen," she said.

Boardman gave CASA the green light to file an amended complaint that addresses the new order by Monday.

Trump calls space station from Johnson Space Center

The president is speaking over the phone to American astronauts on the International Space Station from Houston.

"I just congratulate everybody. And be careful. Be safe. And we love you all," Trump told the astronauts.

He also joked at the beginning of the phone call that many Americans would love to go to the space station, adding, "I wouldn't do it."

The president welcomed the significant others of the astronauts to say hello to them as well and offered to welcome the astronauts in the White House when they return to Earth.

"We're going to see you when you get back. In fact, if you want, Oval Office time, right?" he said.

Kent Nishimura / AFP via Getty Images

Trump presents congressional medals to Artemis II crew

The president participated in a ceremony at Johnson Space Center honoring the crew and staff of Artemis II, giving them each a Congressional Space Medal of Honor.

At the end of the ceremony, a member of NASA presented the president with his own NASA blue crew jacket.

Trump presents a Congressional Space Medal of Honor to NASA astronaut and commander Reid Wiseman. Kent Nishimura / AFP via Getty Images

Trump announces creation of the U.S. Space Academy

During a speech at the Johnson Space Center in Houston, the president announced that he would sign an executive order to create the U.S. Space Academy.

Speaking about the future of space travel, Trump said, "It’s clear that we need to educate and train an entire generation of skilled service members, engineers, civil operators ... and that’s why in a few moments we’re going to get an executive order to begin the process of creating a new national academy. It’s called the U.S. Space Academy. "

He added, "You think of West Point, and you think of Annapolis, and you think of the Air Force Academy, and you think of the Coast Guard Academies. Great, they’re all great, but we’re going to have now the Space Force. We’re going to have an academy for what the people in this room love the most."

The most recently created federal military academy is the Air Force Academy, which was launched in 1954.

Trump arrives at the Johnson Space Center. Kent Nishimura / AFP via Getty Images

Trump’s new Fed chair walks fine line on inflation in key speech

Trump’s new Federal Reserve chair said today that although measures of inflation are still elevated, it is not yet clear that the central bank must take urgent action to address rising prices.

The speech at the Fed’s yearly retreat in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, had been eagerly anticipated after a rocky start to Kevin Warsh’s tenure. Market observers were concerned that he had downplayed the risk of rising prices.

There were also calls for an interest rate hike from economists, including some within the Fed. Trump has routinely called for lower rates that would spark the economy but risk even greater inflation.

Marine One has communication breakdown

We’re learning of a new communications incident involving Marine One while Trump was on board. And the FAA is now moving to fire some air traffic controllers at LaGuardia Airport after last March’s fatal plane crash there. NBC’s Tom Costello reports.

Norway’s King Harald V dies at 89 and his son becomes king

King Harald V of Norway, who went into exile in the United States as a child during the Nazi occupation of his homeland and refused a string of European noblewomen in order to marry his school sweetheart, has died. He was 89.

The royal palace said he died at the National Hospital in Oslo today at 6:35 a.m local time.

King Harald V of Norway in 2019. Francisco Seco / AP file

‘Big questions’ and few easy answers for Trump’s Fed chair at annual retreat

There is a lot riding on Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh’s speech here this morning at the Fed’s storied annual retreat in the Tetons.

Previous Fed chairs have used the annual Jackson Hole address to deliver major policy announcements, and Warsh said last month that he would use the occasion to “frame the big questions” facing the Fed.

But just three months into the job, Warsh faces a growing list of more immediate questions for the central bank he leads.

Judge hits DOJ lawyers with barrage of questions about Kennedy Center renovation and Trump renaming

The judge in a court battle over efforts to add Trump’s name to the front of the Kennedy Center peppered the administration’s lawyers with questions yesterday on their rush to put his name back on it.

The Trump-appointed board at the performance venue voted this month to add the words “renovated and restored by President Donald J. Trump” to the building and to rename the property “President Donald J. Trump Plaza” by Sept. 8.

Trump to phone International Space Station astronauts from NASA Mission Control

Trump will become the first sitting president to call astronauts aboard the International Space Station from Mission Control at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston today.

It’s part of a trip Trump is making to Johnson to award the Congressional Space Medal of Honor to the crewmembers of the Artemis II, who made history this year on their mission around the moon.

It won’t be the first time a president has called the space station, though — just the first time one will have done it from the iconic Johnson Space Center, which has hosted mission control for every crewed NASA mission since 1965’s Gemini 4.

In 2011, President Barack Obama called the space station from the Oval Office, and Trump did the same in 2017, during his first term.

Trump in the past has proposed slashing funding for or privatizing the space station. In a 2018 budget proposal, the first Trump administration suggested ending the U.S.’ involvement in it. Last year, near the start of his second term, Trump in an executive order proposed building a replacement for it with commercial funding.

Americans doubted the Iran war from the start — and Trump’s numbers haven’t gotten better since

Americans remain sour on the Iran war and Trump’s handling of the conflict after six months, and they continue to say they oppose the military action, according to an NBC News review of public polling.

Judge blocks Trump’s Postal Service regulation on mail-in ballots

A federal judge blocked a Postal Service regulation yesterday that would exert control over mail-in ballots ahead of the midterm elections in the latest setback on the issue for Trump.

The recently finalized measure would implement a key provision of the president's executive order on mail-in ballots that would add a new level of bureaucracy to the elections process, which is typically administered by states.

item.title: Trump ‘LOST’ On Stage, ‘DOZES OFF’? ‘Scientist Uncle’ Boast Sparks Mockery At Artemis II Ceremony - The Times of India
item.description: A viral clip from Donald Trump’s appearance at NASA’s Johnson Space Center is drawing fresh online mockery, with critics focusing on an awkward moment when the president appeared to wander across the stage before being directed where to stand. Trump was in Houston on August 28 to honor the Artemis II astronauts and sign an executive order establishing the first U.S. Space Academy.

item.title: Trump to honor Artemis II crew with nation's top space medal - CBS News
item.description:
President Trump plans to award the Congressional Space Medal of Honor to the crew of NASA's Artemis II mission, CBS News has learned.

A White House official confirmed the award will be presented Friday, Aug. 28, at Joint Reserve Base Ellington in Houston.

NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover and Christina Koch, along with Canadian Space Agency astronaut Jeremy Hansen, became the first humans to travel around the moon in more than a half-century during a 10-day mission. They splashed down safely to end the record-breaking flight on April 10.

Only 30 astronauts have received the medal, including Neil Armstrong and John Glenn, according to NASA. Astronauts killed in the Apollo 1 fire and the space shuttle Challenger and Columbia disasters received the medal posthumously.

The last astronauts awarded the medal were Doug Hurley and Bob Behnken, who in 2020 became the first to launch to orbit on a commercial spacecraft. President Joe Biden awarded them the medal in 2023.

Despite its name, the medal is awarded by the president based on recommendations from the NASA administrator. Congress has authorized the president to present, in the name of Congress, a medal to any astronaut who has "distinguished himself by exceptionally meritorious efforts and contributions to the welfare of the Nation and of mankind," according to NASA.

item.title: Artemis II crew to receive top US space medal for historic lunar journey - The Guardian
item.description:
The crew of the historic Artemis II lunar flyby mission have earned the US’s top space medal, officials have announced.

Cmdr Reid Wiseman, pilot Victor Glover, and mission specialists Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen are set to receive the Congressional Space Medal of Honor on 28 August, the US space agency Nasa said.

Nasa’s website indicates that only 30 astronauts have gained the honor – among them Neil Armstrong, the first person to walk on the moon, and John Glenn, who was first to orbit Earth and then served four terms in the US Senate.

Wiseman, Glover, Koch and Hansen were selected for the medal, despite its name, by Donald Trump after the Nasa administrator, Jared Isaacman, recommended them to the president.

The Artemis II crew broke Apollo 13’s record for farthest distance traveled from Earth during their 10-day mission, which began on 1 April. They reached 252,756 miles (406,771km) as they swung above the lunar surface, surpassing the 1970 record of 248,655 miles as part of US plans to again land on the moon – then eventually reach Mars.

Furthermore, Hansen – who is from Canada – became the first non-US citizen to fly to the moon.

“This was not easy,” Wiseman said to reporters after the Artemis II mission safely ended with a textbook splashdown in the Pacific Ocean. “Before you launch, it feels like it’s the greatest dream on Earth. And when you’re out there, you just want to get back to your families and your friends. It’s a special thing to be a human, and it’s a special thing to be on planet Earth.”

The medal ceremony scheduled for Wiseman and his colleagues at the Johnson Space Center in Houston comes four months after Trump hosted the Artemis II crew at the White House. The occasion was marked in part by the president, who turned 80 in June, telling the astronauts: “I would have had no trouble making it – I’m physically very, very good.”

Nasa listed an 11am start time for the ceremony, with a video live stream of the event available at www.nasa.gov/live.

Trump has sought to embrace the Artemis II crew’s achievements despite his administration’s proposal to cut Nasa’s budget by 23%, including a 46% reduction for space science initiatives, for the 2027 fiscal year beginning on 1 October. A House commerce, justice and science subcommittee led by Trump’s Republican party responded by advancing its own Nasa budget proposal that would maintain the science projects the president has been aiming to eliminate.

Beside Armstrong and Glenn, previous Congressional Space Medal of Honor recipients include astronauts who were killed in the Apollo I fire as well as the explosions of the Challenger and Columbia space shuttles.

Douglas Hurley and Robert Behnken were the last astronauts to have been chosen for the medal before the Artemis II crew. Hurley and Behnken in 2020 became the first to launch into orbit on a commercial spacecraft, and they accepted the medal in 2023 during Joe Biden’s presidency.

item.title: Trump to award NASA's Artemis II astronauts the Congressional Space Medal of Honor - Space
item.description:
NASA's Artemis II moon astronauts will join a very exclusive club next week.

President Donald Trump will award those spaceflyers the Congressional Space Medal of Honor next Friday (Aug. 28) at Johnson Space Center in Houston to recognize their historic journey around the moon this past April.

The ceremony will begin at 11 a.m. EDT (1500 GMT) and will feature NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman, President Trump and the Artemis II astronauts. You'll be able to watch it live when the time comes.

Artemis II sent NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover and Christina Koch, as well as the Canadian Space Agency's Jeremy Hansen, on a 10-day trip around Earth's nearest neighbor. It was the first crewed voyage beyond low Earth orbit since 1972, when the Apollo 17 astronauts returned home from the moon.

The mission's success was a huge step for NASA's Artemis program, which aims to establish a base near the lunar south pole in the coming years.

The Congressional Space Medal of Honor is the highest award that the U.S. government can bestow upon an astronaut. It's possible that only Wiseman, Glover and Koch will receive it next week; NASA's media advisory about the event states that Trump will give the medal to "each of NASA's Artemis II crew members," suggesting that Hansen might not be included. (The award is not limited to American citizens.)

Thirty people have received the Congressional Space Medal of Honor to date. They are:

item.title: President Honors NASA’s Artemis II Crew with Highest US Space Award - NASA (.gov)
item.description:
President Donald J. Trump awarded NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, and Christina Koch, and CSA (Canadian Space Agency) astronaut Jeremy Hansen with the Congressional Space Medal of Honor Friday for their service during the Artemis II mission. He presented the awards during a ceremony at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston, honoring the first medal recipients since 2023.

NASA’s historic Artemis II mission launched on April 1, and splashed down safely in the Pacific Ocean on April 10. The crew members were the first astronauts to launch on the agency’s SLS (Space Launch System) rocket, flying aboard NASA’s Orion spacecraft, which the crew named Integrity. During their record-setting mission, the astronauts traveled 252,756 miles from Earth, farther than any humans have traveled before, surpassing a previous record set by Apollo 13 astronauts in 1970. In total, they flew 695,081 miles, including a lunar flyby.

“We gather on these historic grounds to celebrate the immense courage of four intrepid space heroes whose sense of daring and adventure led them further from Earth than anyone has ever traveled ever before,” said President Trump. “Today we’re proudly awarding the Congressional Space Medal of Honor to the remarkable crew of Artemis II. These astronauts did not do it alone. I want to salute all of the engineers, and scientists, launch and landing specialists, everyone at NASA who helped make this mission a great success.”

The Congressional Space Medal of Honor was authorized by Congress in 1969 to recognize an astronaut who in the performance of duties has distinguished himself or herself by exceptionally brave and meritorious efforts, and contributions to the welfare of the nation and humanity. There now are 34 recipients of the award since the beginning of the space program, including the crews of Apollo 1, Challenger, and Columbia who received the award posthumously.

“President Trump’s leadership has put America back on a path to lead the world in space, from creating the Artemis program to giving NASA the resources and mandate to win this new space race,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “The Artemis II crew answered that call with extraordinary skill and courage, showing the world the Moon again and what American leadership and exploration look like at their best. Their achievement was made possible by the exceptional NASA workforce, alongside our industry and international partners, who showed once again what can be accomplished when we commit to big, bold endeavors. We will build on this success as we return to the lunar surface and establish an enduring presence on the Moon.”

The first crewed mission under NASA’s Artemis program paved the way for the 2027 Artemis III test flight in low Earth orbit to demonstrate rendezvous and docking capabilities between Orion and commercial human landing systems, and the Artemis IV mission in 2028, which will return American astronauts to the lunar surface.

“It was the honor of my lifetime to fly on Integrity around the Moon with Victor, Christina, and Jeremy. Having President Trump here at the agency’s Johnson Space Center to honor NASA and my crew underscores the significance of what our teams accomplished,” said Wiseman, who served as commander of the mission. “I can’t wait to see my friends continue this legacy on Artemis III.”

Glover served as pilot of the Orion spacecraft.

“Piloting Orion for the first time in space was a profound honor, made possible because of the years of hard work, dedication, and expertise by countless individuals dedicating their time and talents to the mission,” said Glover. “We share this recognition with the thousands of people who launched us around the Moon and brought us safely back to Earth.”

Koch served as a mission specialist.

“The response to our mission here on Earth was beyond anything we ever imagined and all we ever hoped for. We are grateful every time we hear from people who followed along with our journey. As team members on this shared mission, we accept this award to honor those who made it happen, from factory floors to clean rooms and mission control rooms,” said Koch.

Hansen also served as a mission specialist.

“It is a privilege to receive the Congressional Space Medal of Honor alongside my Artemis II crewmates,” said Hansen. “I share this recognition with the dedicated teams in Canada, the United States, and our international partners who made the mission possible. Artemis II showed what we can accomplish for humanity when we set ambitious goals and work together. For Canada, the mission and the Artemis program as a whole are about much more than just going back to the Moon. It is about the pursuit of excellence and collaboration.”

As part of a Golden Age of innovation and exploration, NASA will send Artemis astronauts on a series of challenging missions to explore more of the Moon and establish a Moon Base on the lunar surface for long-term exploration. These missions will set the stage for sending the first astronauts — Americans — to Mars. Learn more:

-end-

item.title: U.S. President Speaks to Expedition 75 Crew after Awarding Artemis II Crew - NASA (.gov)
item.description:
U.S. President Speaks to Expedition 75 Crew after Awarding Artemis II Crew

President Donald J. Trump awarded the Congressional Space Medal of Honor on Friday at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston to the four‑member Artemis II crew that flew around the Moon in April. During the event, the president also signed an executive order establishing the nation’s first U.S. Space Academy, which will be led by NASA.

Following the ceremony, the president stopped by the Mission Control Center at Johnson and spoke with the Expedition 75 crew aboard the International Space Station as they took a short break from science and exercise research and preparations for next week’s spacewalk.

Flight engineer Sophie Adenot of ESA (European Space Agency) and station commander Jessica Meir of NASA organized the tools they will use during a spacewalk beginning at 7:30 a.m. EDT on Tuesday, Sept. 1. Adenot and Meir also inspected spacesuit components and tethers inside the Quest airlock. NASA flight engineers Anil Menon and Jack Hathaway cleaned the spacesuit cooling loops that keep the suits thermally conditioned and astronauts comfortable during a spacewalk.

Earlier, Adenot pedaled on an exercise cycle while wearing a sensor-packed packed vest and headband measuring her heart rate, breathing rate, and blood pressure. Menon and Hathaway relocated a sample processor and a science freezer as part of scientific maintenance. Meir reviewed her upcoming spacewalking tasks on a computer using 3D animation software.

Roscosmos cosmonauts Pyotr Dubrov and Anna Kikina took turns pedaling on the station’s exercise cycle while attached to electrodes and breathing gear for a routine physical fitness test. Roscosmos flight engineer Andrey Fedyaev synchronized station cameras to Greenwich Mean Time then photographed and videotaped his crewmates as they worked during their shift on Friday.

Learn more about station activities by following the space station blog , @space_station on X, as well as the ISS Facebook and ISS Instagram accounts.

item.title: Artemis II pilot thanks NASA for letting him fly Orion by hand: 'I'm still blown away by that trust' - Space
item.description:
MORRISON, Colorado - The Artemis II crew that circuited the moon earlier this year came full circle, dropping by a distinctive spot on Earth that's visually reminiscent of both the moon and Mars.

On Aug. 3, the vast and stunning Red Rocks Amphitheatre served as both an inoculation of near-term nostalgia and heart-felt congratulations to the crew for the impressive journey of Artemis II. The 10-day mission began on April 1 of this year, flew around the moon and back, and splashed down in the Pacific Ocean on April 10. It was the first crewed flight to saunter spaceward beyond low Earth orbit in 53 years.

Some 8,500 people packed the open-air venue at Red Rocks to make eye-contact with space travelers Reid Wiseman, commander, Victor Glover, pilot, Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen as mission specialists – all of them clearly awestruck by the crowd reaction. The event was a broader post-flight campaign for the foursome, also spotlighting the region's contributions to the sojourn of Artemis II. A science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) fest was also part of the early morning affair.

Iconic location

"I can't imagine a more iconic location on Earth to hear about the trip to the moon," said Robert Lightfoot, president of Lockheed Martin Space and a major aerospace contractor for the Artemis program. There were hundreds of suppliers across the rocky mountain region, over 10,000 employees, that supported the Artemis II mission, he told the gathered throng.

Leadership from industry prime contractors including Lockheed Martin, Amentum, Boeing, L3 Harris and Northrop Grumman took part in the salute to the Artemis II voyage.

Colorado Governor Jared Polis pointed out that "here in Colorado, we're a mile closer to space." As the best and biggest homecoming for the Artemis II crew, he added, "keep reaching for the stars."

Lori Glaze, NASA associate administrator for the Human Spaceflight Mission Directorate, said today "is a truly revolutionary and exciting time for NASA and America's space program. We are going to reach farther. We're going to dream bigger. And we're going to secure America's leadership in deep space exploration and discovery."

What next?

In a pre-event press gaggle, Space.com asked the Artemis II crew members how their Orion spacecraft named Integrity performed and would help the upcoming Artemis III crewed flight in Earth orbit.

"It handled incredibly well," said Reid Wiseman, Artemis II commander. "Just from habitability, I think that is where we learned the most, putting four humans in the spacecraft. We knew that the machine was technically competent and capable of getting to the moon … Artemis I taught us that," he told Space.com.

"We had some heat shield things we needed to sort out on Artemis II. But putting the four of us in there, seeing how the life support system worked and how is it for habitability, to eat, live, work, and sleep in there, we definitely learned a lot that we've handed on to Artemis III," said Wiseman.

Sense of gratitude

The Red Rock Artemis II stage event had the four Artemis II crew members facing a huge gathering of supportive spectators. In excess of 1,300 questions were submitted by the attendees.

The Artemis II crew entrance was marked by roaring footage of the Artemis I launch scored by music from thunderous Metallica's "Fuel."

"The biggest thing that this mission has given us is an overwhelming sense of gratitude. I think we've got to figure out how to keep this going," Glover said.

For Christina Koch, the Red Rocks gathering spurred a call and response audience participation. "I say moon, you say joy," to which the throng promptly called back three times. She also asked the audience to put their thumb out in the air. From a distance, "you can cover the entire Earth with your thumb. That's how small it was to us," she said, "but what you knew was that was home."

Proximity operations

Victor Glover, the pilot of Artemis II, focused on a proximity operations demonstration during the flight. That entailed the crew guiding the spacecraft through a series of controlled approach and retreat maneuvers using the detached upper stage, the interim cryogenic propulsion stage, as a reference target.

"That is when we had a chance to fly the spacecraft by hand, not just using the computers," Glover told Space.com. "We actually got to fly. One of the most amazing aspects of that is looking out the window or through the cameras on the [cockpit] displays to determine how far we were from the upper stage," he explained.

That task made use of all four sets of eyes onboard Orion, Glover said. "We did not have radar, or some other type of digital ranging system between us and that vehicle. But the Artemis II team trusted us to fly like that. I'm still blown away by that trust," he said, "and it flew marvelously."

South pole ambitions

NASA's Glaze added that Artemis III is to fly sometime mid-year in 2027.

"We are going to demonstrate docking with one or both of our two landers, the Blue Origin and the SpaceX lander. They've got some demonstration versions that they are preparing right now. We're working on that mission to prove out, not just going back and forth at a target, but actually docking and doing that hard job," Glaze told Space.com.

Space.com pressed Glaze on the term "demonstration versions" of the Blue Origin and SpaceX lunar landers.

Would the fidelity of those demos be good enough to green-light an actual human moon landing on the Artemis IV mission?

"I do," Glaze responded. "We're working really hard with both of our lander providers on development of the demo pathfinder versions of their landers that we will dock with […] to assure that the docking systems are the same docking system we're going to work with when we are going for the landing mission," she said.

Glaze said that "this is one of the key risks. This allows us to buy down that risk and at least work through that part of the mission. So when we do the landed mission we've got that part out of the way.

"We've got our lessons learned from those docking demonstrations. And then we are really focused on all the risks associated with the landing on the moon … we can really focus our efforts there."

According to Space.com sources, however, there is active discussion of whether the lunar south pole is an advisable location for the first human landing of the Artemis Program. Indeed, Artemis II pilot Glover recently stated that he thinks there's a need to be realistic and progressively work our way to the south pole locale rather than land there first.

"We've had a lot of conversations with both of our lander vendors. The designs they have are for the south pole," responded Glaze. "We're working really closely with them on those designs. And we are very focused on landing at the south pole."

Over the moon

Canada's Artemis II mission specialist, Jeremy Hansen, told the audience that their space trek was a very human experience for the four crew members, "but we came to see and feel you. You shared the moon joy," he said.

Hansen underscored the international character of Artemis II. "It was one of those deliberate contributions to the planet," he said, because billions of us on Earth have to join forces. "We have to work together. We can no longer believe that our end-state is not working together. Not acceptable. We have to collaborate," he said.

Asked by a young audience member about items taken on their excursion around the moon, mission specialist Koch replied: "I took handwritten letters that I hadn't read before from my family, and also a very tall cow figurine. My dad had the idea of having a cow jump over the moon."

item.title: A late Trump keeps Artemis II heroes waiting and then talks more construction - The Independent
item.description:
President Donald Trump on Friday used an award ceremony meant to honor NASA’s Artemis II astronauts to tease the creation of what he described as a “U.S. Space Academy” to be built at an as-yet unannounced site.

Trump signed an executive order to “begin the process of creating a new national academy” as he spoke at the Johnson Space Center and said the new institution would be “a big deal” and one day rival the four existing U.S. service academies which train Army, Navy, Air Force and Coast Guard officers.

“So you think of West Point, and you think of Annapolis, and you think of the Air Force Academy, and you think of the Coast Guard Academy. Great, they're all great, but we're going to have now a Space Force. We're going to have an academy for what the people in this room love the most,” Trump said, referencing his audience of NASA employees and astronauts.

“It'll serve both the United States Space Force as well as NASA and the civilian spaceflight industry, and it'll attract, train, and graduate the very best of our nation, and our nation really has to offer.”

Currently, officers who commission into the U.S. Space Force receive undergraduate education at the U.S. Air Force Academy in Colorado Springs, Colorado. It’s unclear whether what Trump announced would be another military-run service academy or some other type of educational institution.

According to the text of the order released by the White House, what Trump signed does not actually establish any new “space academy” but instead creates a presidential commission to study proposals to create what would be “a NASA-led Federal academy dedicated to combining rigorous technical education with leadership development, discipline, and a durable commitment to public service.”

The president’s comments came moments before he awarded the Congressional Space Medal of Honor to the quartet of Artemis II who became the first humans to leave Low Earth Orbit since the Nixon administration when they circumnavigated the moon this past April.

In what could have been an awkward geopolitical moment, the first of the four to whom Trump presented the medal was Jeremy Hansen, the Canadian astronaut who became the first non-American to travel to the moon.

Hansen politely stood at attention, a Canadian flag visible on his left sleeve, while Trump hung the medal around his neck.

Trump’s comments and his presentation of awards to the Artemis crew came after he arrived for his remarks nearly a half-hour late. He was already in Houston because he had flown there the previous day to fundraise for scandal-ridden GOP Senate candidate Ken Paxton.

He brought up his new construction project twice more during a visit to NASA’s Mission Control center, telling workers there that he’d “just opened an academy” and shortly after suggesting that he’d be “picking a site very soon.”

“Everybody wants it. Every state is fighting for it,” he said.

Moments later, he told the American crew members aboard the International Space Station that he’d announced a “very special academy ... for what you people do” that would be “at the same level” as the existing military academies.
